Title: Circularly‐Polarized Optoelectronic Logic Gates
Text:
RESEARCH ARTICLE

Circularly-Polarized Optoelectronic Logic Gates
Yanji Huang, Yajie Zhou, Junjie Cai, Guangen Li, Zhi Tong, Anqi Li, Jing Lin,
and Taotao Zhuang*
Optoelectronic logic gates, key components in optical computing and optoelec-
tronic integration, are promising for advancing computing performance in the
post-Moore era. Nonetheless, state-of-the-art multifunctional optoelectronic
logic gates still depend largely on complex regulation, showing restricted func-
tionality and intricate conﬁguration. Circularly polarized light oﬀers a promising
route toward highly integrated multifunctional optoelectronic logic gates with
its high-dimensional optics. However, existing circularly-polarized logic gates
are hampered by insuﬃcient discrimination ability and diﬃculty in adjusting
functionality, hindering their applications. Here, a chirality-sensitive pho-
toelectric conversion strategy is demonstrated, and based on which a series of
circularly-polarized optoelectronic logic gates are constructed—encompassing
the majority of logic operations. These devices exhibit an photocurrent dissym-
metry factor of 1.86, underpinning their application in eﬃcient image process-
ing tasks, including stylization and edge extraction. Furthermore, their utility is
extended to simulating max-pooling and realizing chiroptical signal processing
with high recognition accuracy. This work eﬀectively integrates chiroptics and
electronics, paving the way for expanding the horizons of optical computing.
1. Introduction
Light, with its intrinsic optical multidimensions, presents a pow-
erful platform for advancing computation and communication
systems, thereby fulﬁlling growing demands for computational
tasks in the post-Moore era.[1–5] By employing light as inputs
and integrating photoelectric conversion with logic operations,
optoelectronic logic gates (OELGs) are formed, which are key
candidates for next-generation optical computing and machine
vision.[6–10] Although the demand for complex computing has
hastened the emergence of OELGs, they still struggle to meet
practical requirements for multifunctionality and miniaturiza-
tion due to complex control mechanisms, typically wavelength
or voltage regulation.[11–13]
Circularly polarized light (CPL), characterized by its intrin-
sic spin angular momentum (a unique dimension beyond usual

wavelength or intensity), would bring about
promising opportunities for multifunc-
tional OELGs.[14–23] Its left- and right-
handed circular polarization states are anal-
ogous to “0” and “1” in a binary system,
making it an ideal information carrier for
constructing multifunctional OELGs,[24–26]
where diverse logic operations are en-
abled by chiral regulation via photodetec-
tors. However, eﬃcient discrimination of
CPL handedness typically requires integra-
tion of photodetectors with bulky and dis-
crete optical components (such as quarter-
wave plates and linear polarizers), leading
to substantial energy losses and fabrication
complexity.[27] Other solutions, such as CPL
photodetectors (e.g., those constructed on
chiral perovskites, chiral organic molecules,
or chiral polymers), are unable to simul-
taneously achieve ultra-wide wavelength
tunability and high asymmetry, imped-
ing implementation of circularly-polarized
optoelectronic logic gates (COELGs).[28–32]
In this work, we develop a chirality-sensitive photoelectric con-
version strategy for constructing compact and multifunctional
COELGs capable of highly eﬃcient CPL discrimination. These
COELGs show a large photocurrent dissymmetry factor of 1.86
with a wide tunable response wavelength ranging from 400 to
1600 nm, building upon ﬁne integration of a PbS quantum dot-
based photodiode and a cholesteric liquid crystal layer. Their high
performance enables reliable polarization-based logic operations.
We demonstrate up to 9 logic gates by setting diﬀerent photocur-
rent thresholds, connecting photodiodes in parallel, or modify-
ing input conﬁgurations, which are then utilized to construct
image processing units. We further show the multiple applica-
tions of COELGs: stylized image processing (using the process-
ing units), simulation of max-pooling operations in binary neural
networks (via OR gates), and neural network-assisted chiroptical
signal processing (through XOR gates). This work highlights the
potential of COELGs in signal processing and secure optoelec-
tronics, promotes the design and fabrication of multifunctional
optoelectronic hardware, and extends the dimensions of optical
computing.
2. Results and Discussion
2.1. Design of Circularly-Polarized Optoelectronic Logic Gates
Discrimination of CPL states within a single device could en-
able diverse logic operations. We designed a highly eﬃcient

COELG via a chirality-sensitive photoelectric conversion strategy
(Figure 1a). The COELG consists of a cholesteric liquid crystal
ﬁlm (CLC, providing eﬀective CPL selection) and a PbS quantum
dot-based photodiode (achieving wide-wavelength photoelectric
conversion). The CLC layer selectively reﬂects same-handedness
CPL and transmits CPL of the opposite handedness.[33] Then, the
selected light arrives at the PbS photodiode and is converted to
photocurrents with diﬀerent intensities—that is, CPL discrim-
ination. This process could also be seen as the logic comput-
ing: variation in CPL inputs leads to photocurrent discrepancy,
and high photocurrent (HPC) or low photocurrent (LPC) are
equivalent to binary “1” or “0,” which intrinsically aligns with
input or output states of logic gates (Figure 1b). For instance,
right-handed COELG (R-COELG) acts as a NOT gate, whereas
left-handed COELG (S-COELG) functions as a YES gate. Build-
ing on this, we constructed almost all logic gates (taking 9 of
them as examples) by combining left- and right-handed CPL as
dual inputs, and implemented convolutional kernels for image
processing units (Figure 1c). We then employed these COELGs
and units in diverse computing tasks, such as image stylization,
max pooling, and signal processing, showing their versatility
and potential in eﬃcient optical computing and communication
(Figure 1d).
2.2. Circularly Polarized Performance
We then fabricated the designed dual-component-integrated
COELG,
composed
of
a
PIN-type
PbS-based
photodiode
(Au/PbS-EDT/PbS-Halide/ZnO/ITO, Figure 2a,b) and a CLC

spectral range matching the absorption of PbS QDs (Figure
S5, Supporting Information). This led to strong chiral signals
(Figure 2d), demonstrating its potential for CPL photoelectric
device fabrication. Notably, the absorption wavelength of PbS

QDs and the photonic bandgap of CLC were tunable, which
enabled the response wavelength expansion to 1600 nm (Figure
S6, Supporting Information).
Furthermore, we evaluated the photodetection performance of
COELGs (Figure S7, Supporting Information). These integrated
COELGs exhibited distinct photovoltaic eﬀects (Figure 2e,f). They
also generated a chirality-dependent photocurrent (a key opera-
tional parameter), which originated directly from CPL-selective
transmission of CLC ﬁlms. Taking R-COELG as an example:
right-handed CPL was reﬂected while left-handed CPL was trans-
mitted, resulting in low photocurrent under right-handed CPL il-
lumination and high photocurrent under left-handed one; that is,
the chirality-dependent current discrepancy. As anticipated, the
COELGs showed exceptional CPL discrimination in photovoltaic
mode (zero-bias, Figure 2g; Figure S8, Supporting Information).
The fast photoresponse with rise and fall times were 12.3 and
28.4 μs (Figure S9, Supporting Information). The responsivity (R)
was 0.011 A W−1 under 940 nm illumination, with the detectivity
(D*), deﬁned by the equation of D* = R(S)0.5 / (2eIdark)0.5 calcu-
lated to be 1.4 × 1011 Jones. The linear response was evaluated by
linear dynamic range (LDR, 20 × log(Imax/Imin), where Imax and
Imin were the maximum and minimum photocurrents of the lin-
ear range). The COELG demonstrated an LDR of 66.5 dB (Figure
S10, Supporting Information). We also examined its steadiness,
with the photocurrent dissymmetry factor (g-factor) exhibiting
negligible ﬂuctuations, and the maximum photocurrent remain-
ing 92% of the initial after 150 times of irradiation. Figure 2h,i
showed the polarization-dependent photocurrent of the COELG.
Their sinusoidal photocurrent variation with rotation angle 𝜃of
the quarter-wave plate further conﬁrmed a high degree of polar-
ization sensitivity (Figure 2h,i).[36]
These devices also achieved large g-factor values (1.86) as in-
cident light power varied, showing ﬁne light power adaptability
(Figure 2j). Additionally, we fabricated COELGs with diﬀerent
photonic bandgaps, which exhibited good chiral discrimination
ability, with g-factor values of 1.88 at 532 nm and 1.76 at 980 nm

2.3. Image Processing Based on Single-Input COELGs
COELGs selectively recognized diﬀerent CPL and output high or
low photocurrents (HPC or LPC), equivalent to “1” and “0” in
logic computing. For R-COELG: left-handed CPL inputs gener-
ated HPC (“1”); right-handed CPL inputs output LPC (“0”). That
is, R-COELG functioned as a NOT logic gate. On the contrary,
S-COELG acted as a YES logic gate under the same inputs
(Figure 3a,b). These logic gates could serve as basic units of con-
volutional kernels and be applied to image processing: black and
white pixels were inverted when the binary image (“HF”) was
processed by these units (Figure 3c). We then performed im-
age processing, which was also advanced by the linear depen-
dence of the photocurrent of COELG on incident light power
(Figure 3d). Co-regulation of photocurrent direction, handedness
of CPL, and types of logic gates (YES or NOT) enabled the gen-
eration of positive, zero, and negative photocurrents, matching
the processing units’ states of +1, 0, −1 (Figure 3e; Figure S14a,
Supporting Information). We further constructed a 3 × 3 convo-
lution kernel conceptually, where COELG units were integrated
into a pixel array with a readout line, corresponding one-to-one
to the positions of the convolution kernel. The output signals

which COELGs were activated). In this conﬁguration, the pho-
tocurrents were summed in accordance with Kirchhoﬀ’s Law and
subsequently converted to voltage via a transimpedance ampliﬁer
(TIA) for practical applications,[21] promising eﬃcient image pro-

Supporting Information), we achieved edge extraction of “HF”
(Figure 3f,g).
Thereafter, we simulated various image processing operations
using a real captured image (Figure 3h). We presented the images
after color inversion, x- and y-axis edge extraction in Figure 3i–k
and Figure S15 (Supporting Information). Figure 3l showed the
ﬁnal image of edge extraction (combining Prewitt-x and -y), il-
lustrating COELG’s capability to perform image processing op-
erations. Notably, these superior results beneﬁted from the large
g-factor of COELG (1.86, which closely matches the ideal case),
whereas smaller g-values led to poorer performance—as was ev-
ident in sky color discrepancies and suboptimal edge extraction
(Figure S16, Supporting Information). We also performed an im-
age softening operation (Figure S17, Supporting Information),
further conﬁrming the versatility of COELGs in diverse image
processing tasks.
2.4. Dual-Input Logic Computing and Applications
We further developed dual-input COELGs to meet the demand
for more complex optical computing. The combination of left-
(“0”) and right-handed CPL (“1”) inputs could enable diﬀerent
photocurrent outputs (“00,” “01,” “10,” and “11,”,Figure 4a,b).
The variation of output photocurrent thresholds then led to four
logic gates (AND, NOR, NAND, OR, Figures S18–S21, Support-
ing Information). For instance, when the threshold was set at
0.5 μA (above which is deﬁned as “1” and below as “0”), R-
and S-COELGs functioned as NAND and OR gates, respectively
(Figure 4c; Figures S18 and S19, Supporting Information). Sim-
ilarly, when the threshold was set at 0.9 μA, R- and S-COELGs

acted as NOR and AND gates (Figure 4d; Figures S20 and
S21, Supporting Information). We further constructed parallel-
connected devices to enrich logic functions (Figure 4e). Depend-
ing on the photocurrent threshold, (R, R)-COELG achieved AND
or OR logic gates, while (S, S)-COELG realized NAND or NOR
gates (Figures S22 and S23, Supporting Information). Besides,
we achieved IMPLICATION and INHIBIT gates based on (R, S)-
COELG (Figure 4f) for the ﬁrst time: speciﬁcally, with a desig-
nated threshold of 1.8 μA, the COELG generated a high photocur-
rent for inputs “01,” “00,” and “11,” corresponding to the IMPLI-
CATION gate (Figure 4g). When the threshold was set at 1 μA,
the COELG generated a high photocurrent exclusively for the in-
put “01,” which corresponds to the INHIBIT gate (Figure 4h).
Overall, the COELGs showed remarkable performance, featuring
an outstanding dissymmetry factor and an extensive set of logic
gates (Figure S24 and Tables S1–S3, Supporting Information).
Taking the advantages of these COELGs, we showcased the
applications—max-pooling operations in binary neural networks
(BNNs) and chiroptical communication. BNNs are a type of deep
neural network in which weight parameters and activation values
are restricted to discrete binary values (“0” and “1”), signiﬁcantly
reducing energy consumption and computation time required
for calculations.[37] Max pooling retains the most prominent fea-
tures by selecting the maximum value within a local region as
output, thereby decreasing data size and computational com-
plexity. We used OR gates to simulate max pooling operations
in BNNs (Figure 4i; Figure S25, Supporting Information). Tak-
ing partial network segments as examples (“0100” and “0000”):
as for S-COELG, right-handed CPL generated HPC (output 1,
Figure 4j), whereas left-handed CPL generated LPC (output 0,
Figure 4k). This operation transformed a 2n × 2n BNN segment
into an n × n size, mimicking max pooling in BNNs. We further
conducted max-pooling on a complete binary image of “USTC”
(with 150 × 50 resolution), outputting a 75 × 25 resolution image
(Figure S26, Supporting Information). Furthermore, we demon-
strated neural network-assisted information encryption and de-
cryption. Taking signal “H” (with an ASCII code of 01001000) as
an example: deﬁning CPL as input 1 and COELGs as input 2,
they functioned as XOR logic gates for information encryption
(Figure 4l; Figure S27, Supporting Information). The encrypted
signal was processed by the trained neural network to reconstruct
the XOR-encoded output, which was then decrypted by applying
XOR again with the same COELG key, successfully recovering
the original signal “H” (Figure 4l). In the encryption, “accuracy”
was deﬁned as the proportion of perfect reconstruction of the
XOR-encoded output, and “loss” quantiﬁed the discrepancy be-
tween the network’s predicted signal and the ground-truth en-
crypted signal. After 500 epochs of training, the accuracy of the
neural network gradually reached 100% and the loss gradually
decreased. This result veriﬁed the eﬀectiveness of the COELG-
based chiroptical signal processing (Figure 4m).
3. Conclusion
In summary, we fabricated circularly-polarized optoelectronic
logic gates (COELGs) via a developed chirality-sensitive photo-
electric conversion strategy. These COELGs achieved an excep-
tional dissymmetry factor of 1.86 and ﬁne light-ﬁeld adaptabil-
ity over an ultra-wide tunable wavelength range (400–1600 nm).
The outstanding performance derived from ingenious device
design—highly-selective soft helices (chiroptical response) inte-
grated with PbS-based photodiodes (photoelectric conversion).
Enabled by their high performance, the COELGs facilitated a
wide range of logic operations and integrated image processing
units, thereby demonstrating a series of optical computing ap-
plications, such as image stylization, max pooling operations,
and neural network-assisted information encryption. This work
represents a signiﬁcant advance in the design and manufacture
of multifunctional optoelectronic logic gates, expands the opera-
tional scope of logic operations in optical computing, and paves
the way for the development of next-generation optoelectronic de-
vices with enhanced functionality.
